blocks.heading: Cornell Universal Front
rows: How did federal land and railroad policy reshape the West — and at whose expense?
Homestead Act · Transcontinental Railroad · Manifest Destiny · Promontory Summit
I can sequence westward expansion and weigh who benefited and who bore the cost.

blocks.name: Close Read
blocks.lead: Reading type: History Hack-authored instructional synthesis. Not a primary source. Builds SSP.03 (synthesize) and SSP.05 (historical awareness).

blocks.label: Core Path — read one chunk at a time
paras: Sequence the expansion of the United States. The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of free land to settlers who would farm it for five years. Combined with the completion of the Transcontinental Railroad in 1869, these policies accelerated westward expansion as part of Manifest Destiny—the belief that Americans were destined to spread across the continent. The Union Pacific built westward from Omaha while the Central Pacific built eastward from Sacramento, meeting at Promontory Summit, Utah.

Impact on Western Settlement. The Transcontinental Railroad dramatically reduced travel time from months to days, opening the West to settlement, commerce, and resource extraction. Towns sprang up along rail lines, and agricultural products could reach eastern markets efficiently — but this expansion came at tremendous cost to American Indian nations whose lands were taken and whose way of life was destroyed.

Impact on American Indians, Immigrants, and Settlers. Western expansion devastated American Indian communities through forced relocations, broken treaties, and the near-extinction of the buffalo herds they depended upon. Chinese workers who built much of the Central Pacific faced discrimination despite their crucial contributions. The “Buffalo Soldiers”—African American cavalry regiments—served on the frontier, including George Jordan of Williamson County, Tennessee, who earned the Medal of Honor.
